🌍 Land blockade of Iran is impossible: Araghchi

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a land blockade of Iran is impossible given the country’s size and extensive ties with neighboring countries, stressing the need to strengthen national resilience to make sanctions ineffective.

Speaking to IRNA on the sidelines of a seminar for provincial heads of the Foreign Ministry’s offices on Monday, Araghchi said a land blockade of Iran is impossible given the country’s size, the diverse capacities of its provinces, extensive cross-border ties and the historical and cultural bonds between communities on both sides of the borders.
​
The official also added that the provincial offices have been tasked with working with local officials, economic authorities and businesspeople to identify available capacities and establish links with neighboring countries.
​
Araghchi stressed that the country and its people must make enemies lose hope of imposing sanctions and pressure on Iran.
​
The best way to counter such pressure is to demonstrate that sanctions cannot achieve their intended goals and will not be effective, he added.
​
The foreign minister noted that the seminar brought together representatives of all provincial offices of the Foreign Ministry, various ministries and Parliament to discuss ways to carry out their duties under current conditions and further strengthen consular services for Iranians and the country.

Democrats Score a Historic House Majority, Setting Up a Powerful New Chapter in Washington

Democrats are heading into the next Congress with their strongest position in the U.S. House of Representatives in more than two decades, marking a major political shift after a sweeping midterm election victory.

The party has secured at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, following a closely watched North Carolina race in which Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated longtime Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx. 

The Associated Press called the contest in Hubbard’s favor, giving Democrats another seat and pushing their total to a historic level.

The result puts Democrats at their largest House majority of the 21st century. Their current tally matches the 258 seats won after the 1992 election and surpasses the 257 seats they captured in 2008. The party’s gains reflect a broad shift in voter sentiment that reshaped the political landscape across the country.

Republicans, meanwhile, have secured at least 173 seats, with four races still unresolved. One contest remains undecided in each of Tennessee and Minnesota, while two Louisiana races are heading to December runoffs. 

The final balance of power will become clearer once those contests are settled, but the Democratic advantage is already substantial.

The expanded majority is expected to strengthen the position of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is his party’s nominee for speaker. A larger caucus could give him greater leverage in setting the legislative agenda, organizing votes and negotiating with the Senate and the White House.

But a commanding majority does not automatically guarantee party unity. Democrats will still face the challenge of managing differences among moderates and progressives, particularly on spending, immigration, health care and the direction of the federal government.

For Republicans, the results mark a difficult moment of regrouping. Mike Johnson will not return as speaker, while the party conference has selected Jim Jordan to serve as minority leader.

The next Congress will begin with a dramatically altered balance of power in Washington. Democrats will have a historic opportunity to shape national policy, but the real test will be whether they can turn their electoral gains into a cohesive governing agenda.
